sources.body: Gilded Age workers often went without, but across those decades the long trend favored them. Prices for food, cloth, and fuel kept falling while factory pay held fairly steady, so a laborer's dollar bought more in 1895 than in 1870. A machinist's family could now buy ready-made shirts, canned goods, and a clock for the mantel, things their rural parents had made at home or never owned. Factory work was hard, yet many people, native-born and immigrant alike, picked it over tenant farming or village poverty. For many wage earners, industrial capitalism meant a modest but real rise in comfort and choice.

sources.attribution: Lucia Galvez-Reed, historian, The Whistle and the Wage: Work, Power, and Conflict in Industrial America, fictional book, 2015 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a modern labor history)
sources.body: Counting the goods workers bought misses what they lost. Before the factory age, a skilled cooper or iron puddler set his own pace and passed his craft to apprentices. As machines and huge firms spread, owners and foremen took over those decisions. Work was split into repetitive tasks, timed by the whistle, and paid by the piece. A worker who complained could be replaced by another hand. Layoffs during business slumps left families with no savings to fall back on. Wage earners came to see themselves as a separate and dependent class, and they organized and walked off the job more and more often to win back some control.

ush_frq.title: Explaining Union Victory in the Civil War: Material Advantages or Political and Military Choices?

prompt.scenario: Historians have long debated why the United States defeated the Confederacy in the Civil War (1861-1865). Read the two excerpts by historians who explain the outcome in different ways.
requirements: Answer all three parts.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Briefly describe ONE major difference between Ashcombe's and Brennagh's interpretations of why the Union won the Civil War.

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Briefly explain how ONE specific historical event, development, or circumstance from the period 1861 to 1865 that is not explicitly mentioned in the excerpts could be used to support Ashcombe's interpretation.

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Briefly explain how ONE specific historical event, development, or circumstance from the period 1861 to 1865 that is not explicitly mentioned in the excerpts could be used to support Brennagh's interpretation.

sources.title: Historian Lydia Ashcombe on the material foundations of Union victory
sources.attribution: Lydia Ashcombe, historian, Iron, Grain, and Numbers: The Material War, 1861-1865, published 2009 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a modern economic history of the Civil War)
sources.body: The Confederacy did not lose because its generals were outthought or its cause was poorly argued. It lost because it went to war against a society with far more people, far more factories, and a far denser web of railroads. The Northern states could replace a destroyed army; the Southern states could not. Northern farms fed both soldiers and civilians while Northern foundries turned out rifles, rails, and ships year after year. Over four years, this gap widened rather than closed. Brilliant commanders could delay the result, but no amount of daring on the battlefield could overcome a contest in which one side steadily wore down while the other steadily grew stronger.

sources.title: Historian Thomas Brennagh on decisions that shaped Union victory
sources.attribution: Thomas Brennagh, historian, Choices Under Fire: Policy and Command in the Union War, published 2014 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a modern political and military history of the Civil War)
sources.body: Larger populations and bigger economies have lost wars before, and the North very nearly lost this one. Into 1864, many Northern voters were weary and ready to accept a negotiated peace. Victory came from decisions, not from inevitability. Washington chose to turn a war for the Union into a war against slavery, which drew enslaved people away from Southern farms and changed how foreign governments viewed the conflict. Union leaders eventually found commanders willing to press the enemy relentlessly on several fronts at once. Resources mattered, but only because political and military leaders learned how to use them and how to keep a divided public committed to the fight.

sources.body: The suburbs of the postwar decades did not grow out of millions of private choices alone. Their foundation was laid in Washington. ush_frq.title: A Wartime Letter from the Aircraft Line, 1943

prompt.scenario: The following letter was written in 1943 by a fictional African American woman working at an aircraft plant in Los Angeles. She is writing to her sister, who still lives in rural Louisiana. Read the excerpt and answer all three parts of the question.
requirements: Answer each part in complete sentences.
Use specific historical evidence beyond simply restating the excerpt.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Briefly identify ONE claim the author makes in the excerpt about how the Second World War changed work, wages, or opportunities on the home front.

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Briefly explain how ONE specific historical development or circumstance between 1939 and 1945 helps explain why the author was able to get the job she describes.

sources.title: Letter from an aircraft plant worker to her sister, 1943
sources.attribution: Odessa Pryor, a fictional African American riveter at an aircraft plant in Los Angeles, letter to her sister in rural Louisiana, 1943 (ALTON-composed, in the style of wartime personal correspondence)
sources.body: Dear Mae, Eight months now I have been on the night shift riveting wing sections. They pay me more in one week than I made in a month keeping house for Mrs. Pruitt back home, and I put part of every check into war bonds. Hundreds of women here wear slacks and bandanas and do work the foremen once swore no woman could do. When I first came, the hiring office said there were no openings for colored girls. After the government order against discrimination and some pressure from our church committee, they took on a dozen of us. Some of the white men still will not work beside us, and housing is so short that four of us share one room. Still, I am building planes for the boys overseas, and I do not intend to go back to anybody's kitchen when this war is done. Your loving sister, Odessa

a: The author claims defense work paid far more than domestic service, since one week of riveting earned more than a month of housework.
The author claims women were doing industrial jobs, such as riveting, that foremen once said women could not do.
The author claims Black women were hired only after a federal order against discrimination and pressure from community groups.
The author claims discrimination and crowded housing continued even as new jobs opened.
b: Executive Order 8802 (1941) banned discrimination in defense industries and set up the Fair Employment Practice Committee, which gave Black workers grounds to demand hiring.
A. Philip Randolph's March on Washington Movement pressured Roosevelt into issuing the antidiscrimination order, which opened plants that had refused to hire Black workers.
The draft took millions of men into the military, causing labor shortages that pushed employers to hire women and African Americans.

facts: Executive Order 8802, issued by President Franklin D. Roosevelt in June 1941, banned racial discrimination in defense industries and government hiring, and it created the Fair Employment Practice Committee.
A. Philip Randolph's threatened March on Washington in 1941 pushed the administration to issue Executive Order 8802.
Millions of women entered the paid workforce during the Second World War, many in defense industries, and the image of Rosie the Riveter symbolized this change.
The Second Great Migration brought large numbers of African Americans from the South to Northern and Western industrial cities, including West Coast defense centers.
The Pittsburgh Courier promoted the Double V campaign in 1942, calling for victory over fascism abroad and over racism at home.
In 1943, overcrowded war production centers saw racial violence, including the Detroit race riot and the Zoot Suit Riots in Los Angeles.
After 1945 many women were laid off from industrial jobs as veterans came home and war production ended.
President Truman's Executive Order 9981 in 1948 called for equal treatment in the armed forces and led to their desegregation.

samples.essay:
(A) One claim Odessa makes is that the war opened better paying industrial jobs to Black women who used to be stuck in domestic service. She says she makes more riveting wing sections in one week than she made in a month keeping house for Mrs. Pruitt, so war work raised her wages a lot.

(B) Odessa got her job partly because of Executive Order 8802, which FDR issued in 1941 after A. Philip Randolph threatened a March on Washington. The order banned racial discrimination in defense industries and set up the Fair Employment Practice Committee, so when her church committee put pressure on the plant, it had a federal rule to point to. That is why the hiring office went from saying there were "no openings for colored girls" to hiring a dozen Black women.

(C) One effect was that wartime jobs pushed African Americans to demand more rights after the war, building on the Double V campaign for victory over fascism abroad and racism at home. Black workers and veterans who had helped win the war would not accept going back to second-class status, and NAACP membership grew a lot during the war. This helped lead to the civil rights movement of the 1950s, like the Montgomery Bus Boycott in 1955-1956, and it fits Odessa's statement that she will not go back to "anybody's kitchen."

ush_frq.title: A Backcountry Farmer Objects to the Proposed Constitution, 1787

prompt.scenario: The following excerpt comes from a pamphlet written during the public debate over whether the states should ratify the Constitution drafted at the Philadelphia Convention in 1787.
requirements: Answer all three parts.
Each part asks for ONE specific, historically accurate response.
Use complete sentences; an outline or bulleted list is not acceptable.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Briefly identify ONE claim the author makes about the proposed Constitution in the excerpt.

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Briefly explain ONE specific historical development or circumstance between 1776 and 1787 that led to the debate described in the excerpt.

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Briefly explain ONE specific effect that arguments like those in the excerpt had on the United States in the period from 1788 to 1800.

sources.title: A Farmer to His Neighbors Beyond the Mountains
sources.attribution: Pamphlet signed "A Farmer of Tolland Creek," written by a fictional settler in the western Pennsylvania backcountry, late 1787 (ALTON-composed, in the style of Antifederalist pamphlets of the ratification debate)
sources.body: The gentlemen of the seaport towns tell us the new plan will bring order and credit. I ask what it will bring to us who live beyond the mountains. The Congress it creates may lay taxes of every kind, and collectors appointed in a distant city will ride to our doors in years when our grain cannot reach a market. One representative for every thirty thousand souls cannot know the wants of men scattered across a hundred miles of hills. The plan lets that Congress raise armies in time of peace, yet it says nothing to secure trial by jury in civil cases, the freedom of the press, or the rights of conscience. When Massachusetts farmers rose last winter over debts and taxes, the great men called for a stronger hand. Let us not forge the chain they mean to place upon us.

rows.name: Part A

descriptors.0: The response does not accurately identify a claim from the excerpt about the proposed Constitution.
descriptors.1: The response accurately identifies one claim the author makes about the proposed Constitution.

rows.task_specific: Identify one claim from the excerpt about the proposed Constitution, such as broad federal taxing power, inadequate representation, standing armies in peacetime, the absence of protections for rights, or the plan serving the interests of coastal elites.

rows.name: Part B

descriptors.0: The response does not explain an accurate, relevant development from 1776 to 1787 that led to the debate.
descriptors.1: The response explains how one specific development from 1776 to 1787 led to the debate over ratification shown in the excerpt.

rows.task_specific: Explain one specific development from 1776 to 1787 that led to the ratification debate, such as weaknesses of the Articles of Confederation, Shays' Rebellion, postwar debt and economic disputes, or Revolutionary-era fears of centralized power.

rows.name: Part C

descriptors.0: The response does not explain an accurate effect from 1788 to 1800 connected to arguments like those in the excerpt.
descriptors.1: The response explains one specific effect from 1788 to 1800 of arguments like those in the excerpt.

rows.task_specific: Explain one specific effect from 1788 to 1800 of Antifederalist-style arguments, such as the Bill of Rights, state conventions recommending amendments, resistance to federal excise taxes such as the Whiskey Rebellion, or the rise of the Democratic-Republican opposition.

scoring_notes: Each part earns 1 point; the total is 3.
Part A may quote or paraphrase the excerpt, but the response must tie the claim to the proposed Constitution.
Part B must explain how the development connects to the ratification debate; just naming an event is not enough.
Part C must fall in or reasonably near 1788 to 1800 and must link back to concerns like those in the excerpt (rights, taxation, centralized power, backcountry interests).
Do not award Part C for events well after 1800 unless the response clearly ties them to the 1790s.

doc_uses.usable_for: Identifying Antifederalist claims about taxation, representation, standing armies, and missing rights protections
doc_uses.sourcing: A fictional backcountry farmer writing to rural neighbors during the ratification debate. The purpose is to persuade them to oppose ratification, and the point of view reflects frontier distrust of coastal elites and distant authority.

a: The author claims the Constitution gives Congress power to lay many kinds of taxes, which distant federal collectors would enforce on struggling backcountry farmers.
The author argues that one representative for every thirty thousand people is too few to understand the needs of a scattered rural population.
The author objects that the Constitution allows standing armies in peacetime but lacks a bill of rights protecting civil jury trials, freedom of the press, and the rights of conscience.
The author suggests the plan serves coastal elites who wanted a stronger government to put down protests like those of indebted Massachusetts farmers.
b: Under the Articles of Confederation, Congress could not tax or regulate commerce, so it could not pay war debts, and nationalists called for a convention to create a stronger central government. That brought on the ratification fight.

Shays' Rebellion (1786-1787), in which indebted western Massachusetts farmers closed courts to protest taxes and foreclosures, convinced many elites that a stronger national government was needed. That alarmed farmers like the author.

Experience with British taxation and military occupation before the Revolution made many Americans distrust distant, centralized power and standing armies. Those fears show up in the author's objections.
Many Revolutionary-era state constitutions included declarations of rights, so critics expected a national framework to include similar protections and objected when the Constitution lacked them.
c: Antifederalist demands helped bring about the Bill of Rights, the first ten amendments, which Congress proposed in 1789 and the states ratified in 1791. It protected press freedom, religious freedom, and civil jury trials.
Several state ratifying conventions, such as Massachusetts and Virginia, ratified while recommending amendments, which pushed the First Congress to take up a bill of rights.

Backcountry hostility to federal taxation came to a head in the Whiskey Rebellion of 1794 in western Pennsylvania. President Washington sent militia to suppress it, showing the stronger federal power critics had feared.
Fears of centralized power and elite rule fed into the Democratic-Republican opposition to Hamilton's financial program in the 1790s, and later into opposition to the Alien and Sedition Acts of 1798.

common_pitfalls: Treating the author as a Federalist or misreading the excerpt as supporting ratification.
Naming Shays' Rebellion in Part B without explaining how it led to the push for a stronger government.
Citing developments in Part C that fall well outside 1788-1800 without connecting them back.
Saying the Bill of Rights was part of the original Constitution.
Confusing the Articles of Confederation with the Constitution.
facts: The Constitutional Convention met in Philadelphia in 1787 and the Constitution was signed in September 1787.
Article I set representation in the House at no more than one representative for every thirty thousand people.
Shays' Rebellion took place in western Massachusetts in 1786-1787.
The original Constitution had no bill of rights; the Bill of Rights was ratified in 1791.
The Whiskey Rebellion against the federal excise tax on whiskey happened in western Pennsylvania in 1794.
Antifederalists objected to broad taxing power, standing armies, the absence of a bill of rights, and the large size of the republic.

samples.essay:
(A) The author claims that the proposed Constitution fails to protect individual rights, because it "says nothing to secure trial by jury in civil cases, the freedom of the press, or the rights of conscience." He also warns that the new Congress could raise armies in peacetime, so a powerful government with no listed rights could threaten the liberty of ordinary people like western farmers.

(B) Shays' Rebellion in 1786-1787 led directly to the debate. Massachusetts farmers who were deep in debt and facing high state taxes closed courts to stop foreclosures, and the national government under the Articles of Confederation could not raise an army or money to put the uprising down. This convinced many elites that a stronger central government was needed, which led to the Philadelphia Convention, while farmers like the author saw the "stronger hand" as a threat to them.

(C) Antifederalist arguments about missing rights led to the Bill of Rights. Several state ratifying conventions, such as Virginia and New York, ratified while recommending amendments, so James Madison proposed amendments in the First Congress, and the first ten were ratified in 1791. They protected freedom of the press and religion (the First Amendment) and jury trials in civil cases (the Seventh Amendment), which answered the exact complaints in the excerpt.

b: The Townshend Acts of 1767 put duties on tea, glass, paper, lead and paint, and colonial merchants answered with nonimportation agreements in 1768 and 1769, which cut legal imports.
In 1770 Parliament repealed most Townshend duties but kept the tax on tea; the nonimportation movement then largely broke down and merchants resumed importing, which explains the 1771-1772 recovery.

The Tea Act of 1773 let the East India Company sell tea directly through chosen consignees; colonists saw it as a trick to make them accept Parliament's right to tax, forced consignees to resign, turned back tea ships, and destroyed tea in Boston, so legal imports fell.

The Continental Association adopted by the First Continental Congress in 1774 set up a general nonimportation of British goods, enforced by local committees, which explains near-zero imports in 1774-1775.

Boycotts drew women into politics through spinning bees, homespun cloth and pledges to give up tea, linking household buying to the patriot cause.
Committees of correspondence and local enforcement committees spread, building networks that helped organize resistance and, after Lexington and Concord in April 1775, armed conflict.

descriptors.1: The response explains how one specific, accurate development from the period caused or contributed to the trend identified in part A.

rows.task_specific: Students explain one specific historical cause that fits the trend they named in part A. Examples: the Homestead Act's 160-acre claims; federal land grants to railroads under the Pacific Railway Acts, along with railroad promotion of settlement; immigrant recruitment in Europe; new farming technology; drought and falling crop prices around 1890; or the Panic of 1893.

rows.name: Part C

descriptors.0: The response gives no effect, an inaccurate one, or one outside the period or not connected to Plains settlement.
descriptors.1: The response explains one specific, accurate effect of or development related to Great Plains settlement between 1865 and 1898.

rows.task_specific: Students explain one specific effect of, or development connected to, Plains settlement from 1865 to 1898. Examples: Native nations displaced, the bison destroyed, and the Dawes Act passed; farmer protest through the Grange, the Farmers' Alliances, and the Populist Party; railroad regulation through Granger laws, Munn v. Illinois, and the Interstate Commerce Act; the 1890 census report that a frontier line no longer existed; or greater commercial farming for national and world markets.

scoring_notes: Each part is worth one point. Parts are scored separately, but part B must explain a cause of a trend that the data actually show.
In part A, accept an accurate reading of any column. Students do not need to quote exact numbers.
In part B, a bare name such as 'the Homestead Act' with no explanation does not earn the point. The response must show how the development produced the trend.
In part C, accept effects on Native peoples, farmers, railroads, politics, or the national economy if they are tied to western settlement in the period.

contextualization_ideas: The federal government promoted western settlement during and after the Civil War through land and railroad policy.
The Plains Wars and the reservation system displaced Native nations from the land that homesteaders settled.
Farmers on the Plains were tied into national and global commodity markets, which left them exposed to price swings and debt.
outside_evidence: Munn v. Illinois (1877)
Exodusters' migration to Kansas (1879)
Omaha Platform (1892)
1890 census report on the frontier
Destruction of the bison herds in the 1870s and 1880s
reasoning_types: Data analysis: identifying trends in quantitative evidence

a: Population rose from about 410 in 1870 to about 18,200 in 1890, an increase of more than forty times in twenty years.
Railroad track first appears between 1875 and 1880, and population grows fastest after the railroad arrives.
Population and the number of farms both fell between 1890 and 1895, then recovered only slightly by 1900.
The foreign-born share rose to about one-quarter of residents around 1880 and then slowly declined.
b: The Homestead Act of 1862 offered 160 acres of public land to settlers who lived on and improved it for five years, which drew farm families to the Plains and raised the number of farms.

Federal land grants under the Pacific Railway Acts led railroads to build lines across the Plains and to sell land and advertise for settlers, so population grew quickly once track reached the county.
Railroads and state immigration boards recruited settlers in Europe, including Germans and Scandinavians, which explains the large foreign-born share.
Drought in the late 1880s and early 1890s, falling crop prices, and the Panic of 1893 ruined many Plains farmers, which explains the drop in population and farms after 1890.
c: Settlement and railroad building helped destroy the bison herds and pushed Plains nations onto reservations, and the Dawes Act of 1887 later divided reservation land into individual allotments.

Farmers who resented railroad rates, debt, and low prices organized the Grange and the Farmers' Alliances and later formed the Populist Party, whose 1892 Omaha Platform called for government ownership of railroads and free coinage of silver.
Farmer pressure led to state Granger laws regulating railroads, which the Supreme Court upheld in Munn v. Illinois in 1877, and later to the Interstate Commerce Act of 1887.
The Superintendent of the Census reported in 1890 that a frontier line no longer existed, and Frederick Jackson Turner made that report the starting point of his 1893 frontier thesis.

common_pitfalls: Treating the county as a real place or making up real-sounding statistics about it.
Naming the Homestead Act or the railroads in part B without explaining how they caused the trend.
In part C, citing effects from the wrong period, such as the New Deal or the Dust Bowl of the 1930s.
Ignoring the drop from 1890 to 1895 or misreading it as continued growth.
Confusing the Homestead Act with the Dawes Act or with the Pacific Railway Acts.
facts: The Homestead Act of 1862 granted 160 acres of public land to settlers who lived on and improved it for five years.
The Pacific Railway Acts gave land grants to railroad companies, and the first transcontinental railroad was completed at Promontory Summit, Utah, in 1869.
Many Plains settlers were immigrants from Germany, Scandinavia, and other parts of Europe, and in 1879 African American migrants called Exodusters moved to Kansas.
Barbed wire, steel plows, and windmills helped farmers adapt to the Plains environment.
The Dawes Act of 1887 divided reservation lands into individual allotments.
The Interstate Commerce Act of 1887 created the Interstate Commerce Commission to regulate railroads.
The Populist (People's) Party adopted the Omaha Platform in 1892.
The Panic of 1893 began a severe depression.

ush_frq.title: The Market Revolution and American Lives, 1815-1860

prompt.scenario: Between the end of the War of 1812 and the eve of the Civil War, new canals, steamboats and railroads linked farms, towns and cities across the United States. Factories in the Northeast began producing textiles and other goods on a large scale, and farmers and planters grew more crops for sale in distant markets. These developments are often called the market revolution.
prompt.task: Evaluate the extent to which the market revolution changed the lives of Americans between 1815 and 1860.
requirements: Respond to the prompt with a historically defensible thesis or claim that establishes a line of reasoning.
Describe a broader historical context relevant to the prompt.
Support an argument in response to the prompt using at least four documents.
Use at least one additional piece of specific historical evidence (beyond that found in the documents) relevant to an argument about the prompt.
For at least two documents, explain how or why the document's point of view, purpose, historical situation, and/or audience is relevant to an argument.
Demonstrate a complex understanding of the historical development that is the focus of the prompt, using evidence to corroborate, qualify, or modify an argument that addresses the question.

sources.title: Letter from a farmer in western New York to his brother in Vermont, 1830
sources.attribution: Amos Whitcomb, a fictional wheat farmer in Oriska County, New York, private letter to his brother, 1830 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a private letter from a commercial farmer)
sources.body: Dear Brother, Since the canal opened through our valley five years past, a man can haul his wheat to the landing in half a day and see it carried clear to New York. Last fall I sold three hundred bushels at a price we never saw in Vermont. Hannah has given up the loom, for cloth at Pratt's store costs less than her time is worth, and we now have a clock on the mantel and a carpet in the parlor. Yet I own I lie awake some nights. I bought forty more acres on credit from the land agent, and the price of flour is now set in cities I have never seen. When wheat falls, the note at the bank does not fall with it. Our father raised what he ate and owed no man much. I raise what strangers buy, and I owe a good many.

sources.title: Letter from a textile mill worker to her sister, 1846
sources.attribution: Lucinda Marsh, a fictional young woman employed in a cotton mill in a Massachusetts factory town, private letter to her sister on the family farm in New Hampshire, 1846 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a letter from a New England mill operative)
sources.body: Dear Sister, I have put by nearly forty dollars since spring, more money than I ever held at home, and I mean to send some toward Father's mortgage and keep the rest for my schooling. I have a new bonnet and go to lectures at the hall twice a month. But do not believe all the fine things said of this place. The bell rings us up before five, and we stand at the looms near thirteen hours with only short breaks for meals. The overseers now give each girl four looms where we once tended two, and the pay per piece has been cut. Some of us have signed a petition to the legislature for a ten-hour day. I like having my own wages, yet I sometimes think I have only traded one master for another.

sources.title: Pamphlet issued by a textile manufacturing company, 1838
sources.attribution: Treasurer of the fictional Pemberton Falls Manufacturing Company, a promotional pamphlet addressed to New England farm families and state legislators, 1838 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a manufacturer's promotional pamphlet)
sources.body: Parents need have no fear in sending their daughters to Pemberton Falls. Our operatives live in company boarding houses under the watch of respectable matrons, where doors are locked at ten o'clock and attendance at public worship is expected of all. Any young woman found guilty of improper conduct is dismissed at once. The wages paid here exceed what any girl may earn at home spinning or sewing, and many return to their villages with savings, refined manners and improved minds. Our mills prove that American manufacturing need not breed the misery seen in the factory towns of England. By turning the water power of our rivers to useful work, we free the nation from dependence on foreign goods and give honest employment to thousands who would otherwise sit idle.

sources.title: Resolutions of a journeymen mechanics' association, 1835
sources.attribution: Resolutions adopted at a public meeting of a fictional association of journeymen carpenters, shoemakers and other mechanics in Philadelphia, printed in a workingmen's newspaper, 1835 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a labor association's published resolutions)
sources.body: Resolved, that in former days the apprentice learned his trade at his master's bench, lived beneath his master's roof, and might hope in time to keep a shop of his own. Resolved, that the merchant capitalist, who buys labor as he buys leather, has divided our trades into pieces, so that a shoe once made by one skilled hand now passes through many unskilled ones at starvation prices. Resolved, that the custom of working from sunrise to sunset leaves the mechanic no hours for reading, for his family, or for the duties of a citizen in a free republic. Resolved, therefore, that we will labor no more than ten hours in a day, and we call upon all workingmen of this city to stand with us until this just demand is granted.

sources.title: Letter from a New Orleans cotton factor to a planter client, 1854
sources.attribution: Edmund Ravenel Tate, a fictional cotton factor (commission merchant) in New Orleans, business letter to a planter client in Mississippi, 1854; the writer earned commissions on cotton he sold (ALTON-composed, in the style of a merchant's business correspondence)
sources.body: Sir, Your crop of two hundred and ten bales arrived by steamboat on the 9th and has been sold at a handsome figure. The demand from the mills of Lancashire and of New England has never been stronger, and the buyers here say they will take every bale the valley can send. I have charged against your account the plantation supplies you ordered, including the barrels of Ohio pork and corn shipped downriver, and the balance stands in your favor. You write that you intend to purchase more bottomland and to add more enslaved hands to clear it. At present prices I can only encourage you. Cotton is the great business of this port and of the world, and so long as the factories run, the planter who plants more will prosper more.

sources.title: Excerpt from a study of rural America in the canal and railroad era
sources.attribution: Margaret Ellery Sloane, a fictional historian, Markets and Margins: Rural Households in the Age of Canals, 2009 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a historian's monograph)
sources.body: Accounts of the market revolution often move too quickly from the canal boat to the factory gate. In 1860 most Americans still lived on farms, and many rural households in upland districts far from rivers or rail lines continued to grow most of their own food and to trade with neighbors through barter and credit kept in account books. Even families who sold wheat or wool to distant buyers usually did so to protect the older goal of owning land free of debt and passing it to their children. The market reshaped daily routines, the work of women in the home, and the meaning of wages, but it did so unevenly. Its reach depended on geography, class and race, and for the enslaved millions of the cotton South it deepened bondage rather than offering new choices.

defensible_theses: The market revolution greatly changed the lives of many Northern Americans by drawing farm families into commercial agriculture and turning artisans and young women into wage workers, though these changes brought new dependence on distant markets and employers as well as new opportunities.

The market revolution changed American lives to a significant but uneven extent: it transformed the work and households of the Northeast and Old Northwest, while in the South it strengthened and expanded slavery rather than altering the basic labor system.

Although the market revolution reshaped transportation and manufacturing, its effect on daily life was more limited than often claimed, since most Americans in 1860 still lived on farms and many rural and enslaved people saw continuity or deepened constraint rather than new freedom.
contextualization_ideas: After the War of 1812, nationalist policies such as Henry Clay's American System (a protective tariff, the Second Bank of the United States, and internal improvements) aimed to build a national market.
The transportation revolution, including the National Road, the Erie Canal (completed 1825), steamboats on western rivers, and later railroads, cut shipping costs and linked regions.
Eli Whitney's cotton gin (1793) and removal of Native peoples from the Southeast opened lands for cotton expansion, tying Southern plantations to Northern and British textile mills.
outside_evidence: The Erie Canal, completed in 1825, sharply lowered the cost of shipping goods between the Great Lakes region and New York City.
The Panic of 1837 brought bank failures and unemployment, showing farmers' and workers' new vulnerability to market swings.
In Commonwealth v. Hunt (1842), the Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court ruled that labor unions were not in themselves illegal conspiracies.
Gibbons v. Ogden (1824) affirmed federal power over interstate commerce and struck down a steamboat monopoly.
Cyrus McCormick's mechanical reaper and John Deere's steel plow (1837) helped Midwestern farmers produce grain for market.
Samuel Morse's telegraph (first long-distance line 1844) sped commercial information.
Large-scale Irish immigration after the potato famine of the 1840s supplied factory and canal labor and sparked nativist reaction, including the Know-Nothing Party.
The ideology of separate spheres or the cult of domesticity grew as work moved outside the middle-class home.
By 1860 the United States had about 30,000 miles of railroad track, concentrated in the North.
The Lowell mills in Massachusetts recruited young New England farm women, who later organized groups such as the Lowell Female Labor Reform Association (1845).

doc_uses.sourcing: A private letter to a brother has little reason to exaggerate; the writer's mixed pride and anxiety reveal how a middling farmer actually felt about market dependence.

doc_uses.usable_for: Shows young women gaining wages, savings and cultural opportunities while facing long hours, speed-ups, pay cuts and early labor protest.
doc_uses.sourcing: Written privately to a sister on the farm, it offers a candid view that contrasts with company publicity; the writer's goal of helping pay the family mortgage shows ties between farm and factory.

doc_uses.usable_for: Shows the factory system and the moral supervision of female workers; presents manufacturing as opportunity and national independence.

doc_uses.usable_for: Shows the breakdown of the apprentice-journeyman-master system, deskilling under merchant capitalists, and the ten-hour movement.

samples.essay:
After the War of 1812, many Americans felt a new sense of nationalism and wanted the country to depend less on Britain. Henry Clay's American System called for a protective tariff, a national bank and internal improvements like roads and canals. The Erie Canal opened in 1825 and connected the Great Lakes to New York City, and steamboats on the Mississippi made it possible to ship goods upriver as well as down. At the same time, the cotton gin had made short-staple cotton very profitable, so planters pushed into the Southwest. These changes set up the market revolution. Between 1815 and 1860 the market revolution greatly changed the lives of Northern farm families and workers by tying them to distant markets and wages, but those changes brought new debt and dependence along with opportunity, and in the South and in remote rural areas the market mostly deepened older patterns like slavery instead of changing them.

For Northern farm families, the canals changed daily life a lot. In Document 1, a farmer in western New York says that since the canal opened he can ship wheat "clear to New York" and sell it at prices he never saw in Vermont. His wife "has given up the loom" because store cloth is cheaper, and they now own a clock and a carpet. Document 7 supports this, since wheat shipped by canal in Oriska County went from 0 in 1820 to 260 thousand bushels in 1845 while cloth woven at home fell from 310 thousand yards to only 15 thousand by 1855. So families stopped making what they used and started buying it. But Document 1 also shows the cost of this change. Because it is a private letter to his brother, Whitcomb has no reason to brag or hide his worries, so his admission that "the price of flour is now set in cities I have never seen" and that the bank note "does not fall with it" seems honest. This fear was real, because in the Panic of 1837 crop prices and land values collapsed and many farmers who had bought on credit lost their land.

The market revolution also changed work for young women and for craftsmen. Document 2 shows a mill girl who saved nearly forty dollars and goes to lectures, which was a new kind of independence for a farm daughter. Document 3, a company pamphlet, says girls live under "respectable matrons" and return home with "improved minds." However, the purpose of Document 3 matters, because it was written by the company treasurer to convince parents and legislators to support the mills, so it leaves out the long hours. Lucinda's letter in Document 2 was written privately to her sister and tells a different story, with thirteen-hour days, four looms instead of two, and pay cuts, and she says she "traded one master for another." In Document 4, Philadelphia journeymen complain that merchant capitalists have broken their trades into pieces so they can no longer hope to own a shop. Both Documents 2 and 4 call for a ten-hour day, which shows workers in different industries reacting to the same loss of control over their time.

The market revolution did not change everyone's life in the same way, though. Document 5 shows that Northern mills and Western farms were connected to the cotton South, since the planter buys Ohio pork and sells cotton to New England and Lancashire. The factor encourages the planter to buy more enslaved people, but he earned commissions on cotton, so he had a reason to push for bigger crops. For enslaved people, the market meant more bondage, not freedom, as Document 6 also argues. Document 6 also points out that in 1860 most Americans were still on farms and that upland families far from canals still bartered and grew their own food. Even commercial farmers like Whitcomb wanted the old goal of owning land free of debt.

Overall, the market revolution changed American lives to a large extent in the North, where it brought store goods, wages and new labor protests, but the change was uneven. It tied the regions together economically while making slavery more important to the South, which helps explain why sectional tension grew by 1860.

ush_frq.title: Growth and Limits of the Labor Movement, 1877-1900

prompt.scenario: After the Civil War, railroads, steel mills, mines and factories turned millions of Americans and recent immigrants into wage workers. Between 1877 and 1900, workers organized on a larger scale than ever before, through mass strikes, the Knights of Labor, and the craft unions of the American Federation of Labor. By 1900, however, only a small share of American workers belonged to unions, and many of the era's largest strikes had ended in defeat.
prompt.task: Evaluate the relative importance of the factors that contributed to the growth of the labor movement and the factors that limited its success in the period from 1877 to 1900.
requirements: Respond to the prompt with a historically defensible thesis or claim that establishes a line of reasoning.
Describe a broader historical context relevant to the prompt.
Support an argument in response to the prompt using at least four documents.
Use at least one additional piece of specific historical evidence (beyond that found in the documents) relevant to an argument about the prompt.
For at least two documents, explain how or why the document's point of view, purpose, historical situation, and/or audience is relevant to an argument.
Demonstrate a complex understanding of the historical development that is the focus of the prompt.

sources.title: Diary of a railroad fireman
sources.attribution: Private diary of a fictional locomotive fireman in a railroad town in the Appalachian region, July 1877 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a private workingman's diary)
sources.body: July 18, 1877. The notice went up at the roundhouse that wages are cut again, the second time since the panic. A fireman who takes every run the dispatcher allows still cannot pay rent and buy flour in the same month. Nobody planned anything grand at the meeting. We only agreed that we would not take the freight trains out until the cut is taken back. By evening half the town stood at the yard, shopkeepers and miners' wives among them, and they cheered when the engines stayed cold. July 24. Soldiers came in on the cars this morning, sent by the governor, and we hear the federal government has sent troops to other cities. Our grievance is the same as it was last week, but now the papers call us a mob. I do not know whether I will have a place on the road when this is over.

sources.title: Circular of a Knights of Labor local assembly
sources.attribution: Recruiting circular issued by a fictional local assembly of the Knights of Labor in a New England textile town, March 1886 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a labor organization circular)
sources.body: To all who toil in mill, shop, and field. The Knights of Labor ask no man what trade he follows, what church he attends, or what land he was born in. The weaver and the carter, the skilled machinist and the girl at the spinning frame, the white laborer and the colored laborer are welcome in our assembly. Alone, each of us must take whatever wage the corporation offers. Together we can demand the eight-hour day, an end to labor by young children, and the settlement of disputes by arbitration instead of ruinous strikes. We look beyond wages to a day when workers own the shops through cooperation and the wage system itself gives way. Our order has grown by many thousands since the victory on the railroads last year. Come to the hall on Thursday evening and take your place.

sources.title: Editorial on the Chicago bombing
sources.attribution: Editorial in the fictional Lakeport Commercial Advertiser, a newspaper owned by Great Lakes shipping and lumber interests, May 1886 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a business-oriented Gilded Age editorial)
sources.body: The bomb thrown at the police in Haymarket Square has shown the country where the eight-hour agitation leads. For months, foreign-born orators have told our workingmen that employers are their enemies and that property is theft. Now policemen lie dead. We do not say that every member of a labor society is an anarchist. But the honest American mechanic must decide whether he will stand with law and order or with the red flag. Employers in this city would do well to dismiss any man who marches behind agitators, and the legislature should give the police every power needed to break up such meetings before they begin. A man who is dissatisfied with his wages is free to seek another employer. He is not free to stop the wheels of commerce for everyone else.

sources.title: Letter from a craft union secretary
sources.attribution: Letter from the fictional recording secretary of an iron molders' local, affiliated with the American Federation of Labor, to a newly admitted member, 1891 (ALTON-composed, in the style of craft union correspondence)
sources.body: Brother, you will find our dues higher than those of the old Knights, and there is good reason for it. Your money builds a sick benefit, a death benefit, and above all a strike fund, so that when we stop work we can hold out longer than the foundry owner can. We admit only journeymen who have served their time at the trade, because an employer cannot easily replace a skilled molder, while he can fill a gang of laborers by noon. We do not chase schemes to abolish the wage system or march in every political parade. We bargain for wages, hours, and the rules of the shop, and we sign agreements that both sides must keep. This past year we won a raise at two foundries without losing a day. Pay your dues on time and keep the union card in your pocket.

sources.title: Testimony of a steel manufacturer
sources.attribution: Testimony of a fictional Pennsylvania steel mill owner before a state legislative committee investigating the use of private armed guards, 1892 (ALTON-composed, in the style of Gilded Age legislative testimony)
sources.body: I hired the watchmen because the sheriff told me plainly that he could not protect my property. The mill is mine and the stockholders'. I will not have a committee of the union deciding whom I may hire or what machine I may install. When the old scale expired, I offered the work at a rate the market would bear, and the union refused it. That was their right. It is equally my right to hire men who will accept it. Within two weeks of the shutdown I had more applicants than places, many of them newly arrived from southern and eastern Europe and glad of steady work. I bear no grudge against the workingman. My quarrel is with the organizers who tell him that he has a claim on a business he did not build.

sources.title: A historian on courts, troops, and divided workers
sources.attribution: Ruth Tellander, fictional historian, Contested Ground: Workers, Courts, and Capital in the Gilded Age, a fictional monograph, 2009 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a modern labor history monograph)
sources.body: Gilded Age workers did not lack militancy. Again and again, from the railroad yards of 1877 to the Pullman boycott of 1894, they showed that they could stop the most powerful corporations in the nation. What they could not do was outlast an alliance of employers and the state. Governors sent militia, presidents sent federal troops, and federal judges issued sweeping injunctions that turned a strike into contempt of court. Yet the state was not the only obstacle. Workers were split by skill, by language, by race, and by religion. Craft unionists often saw unskilled immigrants as a threat to wage standards, many white unions excluded Black workers, and Chinese immigrants had been barred from entry by law. Employers learned to exploit each of these divisions. The labor movement grew because industrial capitalism created grievances that millions shared, but it remained weak because those millions rarely acted as one.

scoring_notes: Responses may weigh growth and limits unevenly, but they must address both to earn the thesis point.

The table is fictional composite data; credit students who read its trend correctly, such as rising strike numbers in the mid-1880s, a high failure share in 1886-1895, and a growing share of union-ordered strikes, and who link it to the shift toward organized craft unions.

Do not award the outside evidence point for Haymarket, the 1877 railroad strike, or Homestead-style private guards described only as they appear in Documents 1, 3, and 5; outside evidence must add something specific beyond the documents.
A sourcing explanation must say why the source's situation matters to the argument; labeling a source as biased without explaining why does not earn the point.

defensible_theses: The labor movement grew mainly because industrial capitalism, through wage cuts, long hours, and depressions, created widely shared grievances, but its success was limited most of all by employers' alliance with government, which used troops, courts, and injunctions to break major strikes.

Government repression mattered, but divisions among workers by skill, ethnicity, and race were the most important limit, as shown by the AFL's choice to organize only skilled workers and leave out the unskilled immigrants and Black workers whom the Knights had welcomed.

Public fear of radicalism after Haymarket was the turning point: it helped destroy the Knights of Labor and pushed organized labor toward the narrow but more durable 'pure and simple' unionism of the AFL, which brought gains to some skilled workers and left most workers unorganized.
contextualization_ideas: Rapid industrialization after the Civil War, the growth of national railroads and huge firms such as Carnegie Steel and Standard Oil, and the shift from independent artisans to wage labor in large workplaces.
Depressions following the Panic of 1873 and the Panic of 1893 brought wage cuts, layoffs, and unemployment that set off mass strikes and protests such as Coxey's Army in 1894.
Laissez-faire ideas, Social Darwinism, and the gospel of wealth shaped a public and judicial outlook that treated unions as threats to property and to freedom of contract.
outside_evidence: The Great Railroad Strike of 1877 began over wage cuts on the Baltimore and Ohio Railroad, spread to many cities, and was put down with state militia and federal troops sent by President Rutherford B. Hayes.

The Knights of Labor, led by Terence Powderly from 1879, grew to roughly 700,000 members by 1886 after a successful strike against Jay Gould's railroads in 1885, then declined quickly after Haymarket and the failed Southwest railroad strike of 1886.
Samuel Gompers led the American Federation of Labor, founded in 1886, which organized skilled workers by craft and focused on wages, hours, and working conditions.

In the Homestead Strike of 1892, Carnegie Steel under Henry Clay Frick brought in Pinkerton guards, the state militia was called out, and the Amalgamated Association of Iron and Steel Workers was broken.

In the Pullman Strike of 1894, the American Railway Union led by Eugene V. Debs supported a boycott; President Grover Cleveland sent federal troops, a federal court issued an injunction, and the Supreme Court upheld it in In re Debs in 1895.
The Sherman Antitrust Act of 1890 was used by federal courts against labor unions as combinations in restraint of trade.
The Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882, backed by many white workers, barred Chinese laborers from entering the United States.
Employers used blacklists, yellow-dog contracts, lockouts, and replacement workers to resist unions.
The Haymarket affair of May 1886 followed nationwide eight-hour demonstrations beginning May 1, and the trial and execution of anarchists fed a Red Scare against labor.
reasoning_types: Comparison of the Knights of Labor and the AFL

doc_uses.usable_for: Wage cuts after the Panic of 1873 as a cause of mass, often spontaneous strikes with community support; troops as a limit on labor success.
doc_uses.sourcing: A private diary, not written for publication, gives a candid view of the grievance and the fear of losing work; its lack of a public purpose makes its account of community support and the shift in press coverage believable, though it shows only one worker's view.

doc_uses.usable_for: Growth of an inclusive mass organization that crossed lines of skill, sex, and race; reform goals like the eight-hour day, cooperatives, and arbitration; mention of the 1885 railroad victory as a cause of growth.
doc_uses.sourcing: As a recruiting circular, it aims to attract members and so stresses unity and success; its broad goals of ending the wage system help explain why the Knights struggled to win concrete gains and avoided strikes.

doc_uses.usable_for: Haymarket and public fear of radicalism and of immigrants as a limit on labor; employer calls for dismissals and police power.
doc_uses.sourcing: The paper's owners are shipping and lumber employers, so its purpose is to discredit organized labor and the eight-hour movement by tying it to anarchism and foreigners; that matters because such press coverage shaped middle-class opinion against unions.

doc_uses.usable_for: The AFL's craft unionism as a strategy that brought durable gains through dues, benefits, strike funds, and contracts; exclusion of the unskilled as a limit on the size of the movement.
doc_uses.sourcing: Written to a new member to justify high dues and narrow aims, it presents craft unionism in the best light; the secretary's position explains the open comparison with the Knights and the dismissive attitude toward unskilled laborers.

doc_uses.usable_for: Employer power, private guards, the right to manage, and the use of new immigrants as replacement workers as limits on labor.
doc_uses.sourcing: The owner is defending himself before a legislative investigation, so he frames armed guards as necessary protection and stresses property rights; his situation helps explain both his claim to bear no grudge and his reliance on a surplus of immigrant labor.

doc_uses.usable_for: Overview argument that shared grievances drove growth while state intervention (troops, injunctions) and divisions by skill, race, ethnicity, and religion limited success.
doc_uses.sourcing: A modern historian writing with hindsight weighs multiple causes; students can use it to frame a ranking of factors, while noting that it is an interpretation rather than period evidence.

doc_uses.usable_for: Rising strike activity in the mid-1880s, high failure rates during 1886-1895 when Haymarket, Homestead, and Pullman occurred, and a growing share of union-ordered strikes, with better outcomes late in the period, consistent with the rise of organized craft unions.
doc_uses.sourcing: A state labor bureau's statistics count reported strikes and sort them into simple outcome categories; the data show patterns but not causes, and the meaning of partial success is unclear.

common_pitfalls: Describing strikes one by one without weighing which factors mattered most for growth and for limited success.
Addressing only why labor failed and ignoring why the movement grew.
Treating the Knights of Labor and the AFL as the same type of organization, or claiming the AFL organized unskilled industrial workers.
Placing events outside the period, such as the Wagner Act or CIO, as evidence for 1877-1900 rather than as later connections.
Calling Document 3 or Document 5 biased without explaining how the author's interests shape the argument.
Treating Document 7 as real national statistics instead of a fictional composite state sample.
facts: The Great Railroad Strike of 1877 began in July 1877 after wage cuts on the Baltimore and Ohio Railroad, and federal troops were used to end it.
The Knights of Labor was founded in 1869, admitted skilled and unskilled workers, women, and Black workers, and peaked in membership around 1886.
The Haymarket Square bombing in Chicago took place on May 4, 1886, during the eight-hour movement.
The American Federation of Labor was founded in 1886, and Samuel Gompers led it for most of its early history.
The Homestead Strike against Carnegie Steel took place in 1892 and involved a battle with Pinkerton guards.
The Pullman Strike of 1894 involved the American Railway Union under Eugene V. Debs and was ended by federal troops and a court injunction upheld in In re Debs (1895).
The Chinese Exclusion Act was passed in 1882.
The Sherman Antitrust Act was passed in 1890 and was later applied against labor unions.
Panics in 1873 and 1893 set off serious depressions with wage cuts and high unemployment.

samples.essay:
After the Civil War the United States industrialized faster than almost any country in history. Railroads connected the continent, and men like Andrew Carnegie and John D. Rockefeller built huge corporations that used new machines and cheap labor. Millions of immigrants, more and more from southern and eastern Europe, came looking for work in mills and mines. Depressions after the Panic of 1873 and again in 1893 led to wage cuts and layoffs, and most judges and politicians believed in laissez-faire and Social Darwinist ideas that said the government should not interfere between employers and workers. Because of this, workers had serious grievances but very little protection, which is why they tried to organize.

The labor movement grew mainly because industrial capitalism created shared grievances like wage cuts and long hours, and because organizations like the Knights of Labor and the AFL gave workers a way to act together. However, its success was limited more by the alliance of employers with the government, which used troops and courts to break strikes, than by anything else, although divisions among workers by skill, race, and nationality made that power easier to use.

The biggest reason labor grew was economic hardship. In Document 1, a railroad fireman writes in 1877 that wages were cut "the second time since the panic" and that he cannot pay rent and buy flour in the same month. Since this is a private diary, he had no reason to exaggerate for an audience, so it shows the strike started from real need and not from planning by radicals, as he says "Nobody planned anything grand." The whole town supported the strikers, which shows how widely the grievances were shared. Organizations then turned this anger into membership. Document 2, a Knights of Labor circular, welcomes workers of any trade, religion, or race and calls for the eight-hour day and cooperation. Its purpose is recruiting, so it probably makes the Knights sound more united and successful than they were, but its claim that the order "has grown by many thousands" after a railroad victory fits with the Knights growing to around 700,000 members by 1886. Document 7 also shows growth, since strikes more than doubled from 212 in 1881-1885 to 486 in 1886-1890 and the share ordered by unions rose from 41 to 72 percent.

The main limit on labor's success was government power on the side of employers. In Document 1 the governor sends soldiers and the federal government sends troops, and the papers suddenly "call us a mob." Document 6, a historian, argues that workers "could not outlast an alliance of employers and the state," pointing to militia, troops, and injunctions. A clear example is the Pullman Strike of 1894, when President Cleveland sent federal troops to Chicago and a federal court issued an injunction against the American Railway Union, using the Sherman Antitrust Act. Eugene Debs went to jail, and the Supreme Court upheld this in In re Debs (1895). Public opinion also turned against labor after violence. Document 3, an editorial after Haymarket, links the eight-hour movement to anarchists and tells employers to fire marchers. Because the paper was owned by shipping and lumber interests, its purpose was to protect business by making unions look foreign and dangerous, and that kind of fear helped destroy the Knights after 1886. Document 7 shows that failures outnumbered successes in 1886-1895, the years of Haymarket and Pullman.

Still, divisions among workers also mattered. Document 5, a steel owner, says he had more applicants than jobs, "many of them newly arrived from southern and eastern Europe." He is defending himself before a committee investigating armed guards, so he wants to look reasonable, but his testimony shows how immigration gave employers replacement workers. Document 6 adds that many unions excluded Black workers and Chinese immigrants were barred by law. In Document 4, the AFL molders only admit skilled journeymen. This craft strategy actually worked for the skilled, winning raises "without losing a day," and Document 7 shows more successes in 1896-1900 as union-ordered strikes grew. But it left out most unskilled workers, so the same choice that made the AFL survive is also why so few workers were in unions by 1900.

In conclusion, hard conditions made workers organize, but the government's support for employers did the most to stop them, with worker divisions making it worse.

samples.essay:
The labor movement between 1877 and 1900 grew for many reasons and it also faced many problems. Workers had a lot of reasons to organize, but employers and other things made it hard for unions to succeed. In this essay I will talk about the factors that helped the labor movement grow and the factors that limited it.

After the Civil War the United States changed a lot. Factories and railroads got bigger and many people came from other countries to work in them. Workers were not paid well and many of them were unhappy, so they started to form groups.

Document 1 shows a railroad fireman whose wages were cut two times. The workers in his town refused to take the trains out and the whole town cheered for them. But then soldiers came in and the papers called the workers a mob. This shows that workers wanted to organize because of low wages but the government sent troops against them. Document 2 is a Knights of Labor circular that says everyone is welcome no matter their trade or race. It says they want an eight hour day. This shows why the Knights grew, because they let in many kinds of workers.

Document 3 is an editorial about Haymarket. It says that foreign born orators are dangerous and employers should fire anyone who marches with agitators. This shows that business people were against unions and blamed them for violence. Document 5 shows a steel mill owner who hired guards and new immigrants when the union refused his pay rate. So employers could replace strikers easily, which limited the unions.

Document 4 says the craft unions had higher dues and a strike fund, and only let in skilled workers. Document 7 shows that the number of strikes went up in 1886 to 1890 and many of them failed, but more of them were ordered by unions over time.

In conclusion, the labor movement grew because of bad conditions in industry, but it was limited because employers and the government were stronger than the workers.

sources.title: Letter from a homeowner to the President
sources.attribution: Letter from Mrs. Agnes Pavlik, wife of a laid-off glassworker, Toledo, Ohio, to the President of the United States, November 1934 (ALTON-composed, in the style of letters written by ordinary citizens to the White House during the Depression)
sources.body: Dear Mr. President, I am not an educated woman so please excuse my writing. My husband worked eleven years at the glass plant until they let him go in 1931. By last spring the bank was ready to take our house, the only thing we ever owned. Then the Home Owners' Loan Corporation took over our mortgage at a lower rate, and we are still under our own roof. My mother says no government ever did a thing for working people before, only for the rich ones. I listen to you on the radio every time, and it feels like you are talking right to our kitchen. Now I must ask one more thing. Our boy Stanley is nineteen and has looked for work for two years. Is there some government job for a strong young man? We do not want charity, only a chance. God bless you and your family.

sources.title: Diary of a Civilian Conservation Corps enrollee
sources.attribution: Private diary of Raymond Hollis, age 18, an enrollee from Pittsburgh at a Civilian Conservation Corps camp in western Pennsylvania, entries from May 1935 (ALTON-composed, in the style of personal diaries kept by CCC enrollees)
sources.body: May 4. Planted pine seedlings on the burned ridge all day. My hands are raw but I ate three plates at supper. Most of the fellows are city boys like me. The Army lieutenant runs the camp like a regiment, bugle at six, inspection, lights out. May 11. Pay day. Thirty dollars, and twenty-five goes straight home to Ma. She wrote that it pays the rent and the coal man. First time since Pop died that she is not behind. May 19. One fellow says the government is just keeping us off the streets so we don't make trouble. Maybe so. But I learned to run a crosscut saw and to read a map, and the foreman says I might drive truck next month. I never figured Washington knew Pittsburgh existed, let alone a fellow like me.

sources.title: Editorial in a manufacturers' newspaper
sources.attribution: Editorial in The Commonwealth Ledger, a weekly newspaper published by an association of New England manufacturers, October 1936 (ALTON-composed, in the style of business-sponsored editorials opposing the New Deal during the 1936 campaign)
sources.body: Beginning in January, every man and woman on a factory payroll will carry a federal number and see a federal tax taken from wages. The Social Security Act is advertised as protection for old age. Read it closely and you find something else: a permanent bureau in Washington that will keep a ledger on every working citizen for the rest of his life. Meanwhile relief rolls swell, and an army of federal agents tells farmers what to plant and employers whom to bargain with. The founders built a government of limited powers, and the states and the family were to care for their own. Today the citizen is taught to look to Washington for his pension, his job and his wages. A people that learns dependence will not easily unlearn it. In November the voters must decide whether they remain citizens or become clients.

sources.title: Statement of a tenant farmer
sources.attribution: Statement by Josiah Freeman, a Black sharecropper in eastern Arkansas, recorded at a meeting of a tenant farmers' organization, February 1937 (ALTON-composed, in the style of testimony given by Southern tenant farmers during the 1930s)
sources.body: They tell us the government in Washington is helping the farmer. I have farmed cotton on the same place for sixteen years, and I have not seen that help. When the government paid to plow under cotton and plant less, the check went to the man who owns the land. He was supposed to share it with his tenants. He kept most of it. Then, with fewer acres in cotton, he told three families on our place to move on, mine among them. We went to the county committee to complain, and the county committee is made up of landowners. A man from Washington came through once and wrote down what we said, and that was all we heard. I am told there is relief work in town now. I want to believe Washington means well by people like us. But down here it comes through the same hands it always did.

sources.title: Resolution of an industrial union local
sources.attribution: Resolution adopted by Local 417 of an industrial union affiliated with the Committee for Industrial Organization, Harmon, Ohio, a fictional steel town, June 1937 (ALTON-composed, in the style of union local resolutions of the late 1930s)
sources.body: Whereas, for forty years the workers of the Harmon mills had no voice in setting their wages or hours, and any man who spoke for a union risked his job; and Whereas, the National Labor Relations Act now makes it the law of the land that working people may organize and bargain through representatives of their own choosing; and Whereas, in an election supervised by the National Labor Relations Board, a majority of the men in the mills chose this local as their bargaining agent; Therefore be it resolved, that this local thanks the national government for standing between the worker and the company spy; that we urge every member to register and vote in all elections to defend these rights; and that we warn the company that the Board's ruling binds it, and its old methods of the blacklist and the discharge slip are now outside the law.

sources.title: Historian's interpretation of federal power
sources.attribution: Excerpt from Miriam Oduya, Washington Comes to Main Street: Federal Power and Local Life, 1933-1948, a fictional work of history, 2011 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a scholarly monograph on American political history)
sources.body: The New Deal made the federal government visible to ordinary Americans as never before. Its presence was real but uneven. Relief checks, work projects and farm payments mostly passed through county officials, state agencies and local committees. Those local hands decided who was deserving, and in much of the country they drew the color line. The Social Security Act left out agricultural and domestic workers, who were disproportionately Black and female. The legislation built a framework of national responsibility without fully displacing older local hierarchies. Wartime mobilization did more to make federal power routine. After 1942 most wage earners had income tax withheld from their pay, young men registered for the draft, and families lived under federal ration books. By 1945 the relationship that the New Deal had opened as an emergency had become a permanent feature of American life.

defensible_theses: The New Deal changed the relationship between the federal government and ordinary Americans to a large extent. Washington took direct responsibility for relief, jobs, home mortgages, old-age security, and workers' right to organize, and many citizens came to look to the national government for economic security.

The New Deal changed the relationship only to a moderate extent. Federal programs reached millions, but they were often administered locally and kept existing racial, regional, and gender hierarchies in place, so Black sharecroppers, domestic workers, and many women gained much less than white industrial workers.
The New Deal began a lasting change, but World War II completed it. Wartime income tax withholding, the draft, rationing, and the GI Bill made federal power a routine part of everyday life by 1945.
contextualization_ideas: The Great Depression after the 1929 crash: about 25 percent unemployment by 1933, bank failures, and the collapse of private charity and local and state relief.

Before 1933, federal contact with most citizens was limited mainly to the post office and tariffs, and the Hoover administration emphasized voluntarism and indirect aid such as the Reconstruction Finance Corporation.

Progressive Era precedents such as the Federal Reserve, the federal income tax under the Sixteenth Amendment, and federal regulation of food and drugs, along with wartime mobilization in 1917-1918, which prepared the ground for broader federal action.
outside_evidence: The Banking Act of 1933 created the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, which insured individual bank deposits.
The Works Progress Administration (1935) employed millions of people. Its Federal Writers', Art, and Theatre projects also employed artists and writers.
The Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938 set a national minimum wage of 25 cents an hour, limited the workweek, and restricted child labor.

In Schechter Poultry Corp. v. United States (1935), the Supreme Court struck down the National Industrial Recovery Act. In United States v. Butler (1936), it invalidated the original Agricultural Adjustment Act's processing tax.
Franklin Roosevelt's 1937 plan to add justices to the Supreme Court failed, and a conservative coalition of Republicans and Southern Democrats limited further New Deal legislation after 1938.
The Indian Reorganization Act of 1934 ended allotment and encouraged tribal self-government.
Executive Order 8802 (1941) banned discrimination in defense industries and created the Fair Employment Practices Committee.
The Servicemen's Readjustment Act (GI Bill) of 1944 provided education, home loan, and unemployment benefits to veterans.
The Current Tax Payment Act of 1943 introduced wage withholding, and wartime revenue laws greatly expanded the number of income tax payers.
Critics such as the American Liberty League attacked the New Deal from the right, while Huey Long's Share Our Wealth movement and the Townsend Plan pushed for more radical federal action.
Japanese American incarceration under Executive Order 9066 (1942) showed how far federal power over individuals could extend in wartime.
reasoning_types: Comparison (among groups and between the New Deal and wartime)

doc_uses.usable_for: Direct federal help through HOLC mortgage refinancing, a new expectation that Washington would help working people, and the personal bond created by radio fireside chats.
doc_uses.sourcing: The letter is addressed to the President by a citizen asking for a job for her son. Her purpose may lead her to stress gratitude and deservingness. That makes it strong evidence of new expectations of the federal government, but weaker evidence of how well the programs worked.

doc_uses.usable_for: The CCC as direct federal employment of young men, with wages sent home to families and skills training, and the sense that Washington now recognized ordinary people.
doc_uses.sourcing: A private diary was not written to persuade, which makes it fairly candid. It also records a skeptic's view that the CCC was a form of social control. The enrollee is a white urban youth, which limits how far his experience can be generalized.

doc_uses.usable_for: Conservative opposition to Social Security, relief, the AAA, and labor law as an unconstitutional expansion of federal power that would create dependency. It also confirms how much contact with Washington had grown.
doc_uses.sourcing: The editorial was published by manufacturers who faced payroll taxes and union bargaining, and it appeared during the 1936 election campaign. Its purpose was to sway voters, so it may exaggerate federal intrusion.

doc_uses.usable_for: Limits of the New Deal: AAA payments went to landowners, tenants were displaced, and locally controlled administration preserved racial and class hierarchies in the South.
doc_uses.sourcing: The speaker is a Black sharecropper speaking at a tenant organization meeting, where the goal was to document grievances. His exclusion from benefits shapes his view, and that view is valuable because such voices rarely appear in official records.

doc_uses.usable_for: The Wagner Act and NLRB made the federal government a protector of workers' right to organize, and labor's political loyalty grew as a result.
doc_uses.sourcing: A union resolution celebrating a victory under federal law has a clear interest in praising the NLRB and in mobilizing members politically. Its audience includes both members and the employer.

doc_uses.usable_for: Quantitative evidence that federal contact grew through work relief and Social Security accounts in the 1930s. Work relief declined as the war began, while income tax filing rose sharply in the 1940s, which supports the argument that wartime mobilization extended the change.
doc_uses.sourcing: These are fictional composite county data drawn from federal agency reports. They show the scale of contact but not its quality, and they do not show who was excluded.

doc_uses.usable_for: A historian's qualified argument: the New Deal made federal power visible but uneven because of local administration and exclusions from Social Security, and the war made federal power routine.
doc_uses.sourcing: This is a later scholarly interpretation written with hindsight. It can corroborate Document 4 and the table and help frame an argument that weighs change against continuity.

common_pitfalls: Listing New Deal programs without evaluating how much they changed the federal-citizen relationship.
Treating the New Deal as helping all Americans equally and ignoring exclusions by race, region, and gender.
Ending the analysis in 1938 and leaving out the wartime years through 1945.
Summarizing documents without connecting them to an argument, or calling the author's identity sourcing without explaining why it matters.
Misdating programs or confusing them, for example placing the WPA in 1933 or treating the CCC as open to women.
Treating the fictional county data or the fictional historian as real national statistics or published scholarship.
facts: The Civilian Conservation Corps (1933) employed young men on conservation projects. Enrollees earned 30 dollars a month, and 25 dollars of it was sent to their families.
The Home Owners' Loan Corporation (1933) refinanced home mortgages that were in danger of foreclosure.
The Agricultural Adjustment Act (1933) paid farmers to reduce production. In the South, payments often went to landowners, and many tenants and sharecroppers were displaced.
The Social Security Act (1935) created old-age insurance funded by payroll taxes that began in 1937, along with unemployment insurance. It originally excluded agricultural and domestic workers.
The National Labor Relations Act (Wagner Act) of 1935 protected the right to organize and bargain collectively and created the National Labor Relations Board to hold union elections.
The Works Progress Administration was created in 1935 and ended in 1943.
Franklin Roosevelt used radio fireside chats, beginning in 1933, to speak directly to Americans.
Unemployment was roughly 25 percent in 1933.
During World War II, the income tax was expanded to most wage earners, and withholding began under the Current Tax Payment Act of 1943.
The GI Bill was enacted in 1944.
